prize_parts.citation: for a poetry, from Purgatory and Anteparadise onward, that makes mourning, the damaged body and the national landscape into the material of a radically formal and sustained poetic architecture

statement.case_for: My preferred writer is unchanged, but the configuration has changed in one respect: the citation now names only the poems. The chair's questions and my colleagues' objections show that the landscape-scale and sky-writing interventions cannot be weighed as literature on the evidence we have. They belong to context. On public knowledge, the case for Zurita rests on the printed sequences: Purgatory and Anteparadise, and the later books as I understand them (La vida nueva and INRI). These books are textual in conception. A violated body, a ruined landscape and collective mourning are given a recurring, almost liturgical diction and a visionary imagery that is sustained over about five decades. Under the common criteria this seems to me the most distinctive voice and the most radical formal conception on the shortlist. The imaginative and ethical seriousness does not depend on the Chilean subject alone, and the project has kept transforming its own means. My claim therefore covers the whole oeuvre and not one celebrated sequence or event. I have not read these texts afresh or independently verified any source for this stage. This is a judgment from public knowledge, and I hold it with the limits stated below.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation remains that poetry travels worst in translation, so the sequences, their typography and their repetition are hard to judge outside Spanish. My knowledge of the later books is thinner than my knowledge of the early sequences, so sustained quality across the whole career is partly an inference. Four colleagues (Mattson, Palm, Sem-Sandberg and Swärd) doubt that the case can be separated securely from the extra-textual interventions and from the historical weight of the Chilean context. I cannot fully dispel that doubt from public knowledge. Cărtărescu's case is more evenly distributed across a large body of prose, and his supporters make a serious argument about unity and scale. If the committee cannot anchor Zurita in the printed poems, Cărtărescu is the natural alternative, and I would not regard that outcome as a defeat for the criteria. I also keep in view that my scholarly work on modern poetry, the fragment and exile literature may incline me towards poetry, and I should not mistake familiarity with the genre for superior merit.

responses.point: Palm ranks Cărtărescu first and Zurita sixth. She wants the committee to be confident that the written sequences carry the case before the preference moves to Zurita, and she keeps the boundary between literature and non-literary art practice as a question for the criteria.
responses.response: That condition is fair and I have tried to meet it. The citation now names the poems and the sequences, and it omits the extension into public space that appeared in my round-1 wording. I answer the chair's first question by saying that the case should stand on the printed books, and I accept that a reader who is not persuaded by the poems should not be persuaded by the interventions. I cannot demonstrate the strength of the poems to you through translation, and I will not pretend to. I accept your point that I cannot settle it from public knowledge alone. Your test for Cărtărescu, whether the late books extend the project or merely enlarge it, is the same kind of test I apply to Zurita's later books. I would apply the same standard of evidence to both.

responses.point: Swärd ranks Can Xue first, and she says translation risk applies to Can Xue at least as strongly as to Cărtărescu. She insists that consistency of method is not by itself a lack of depth, and that the question is whether each book re-examines perception and selfhood or only restages them.
responses.response: I accept the correction. In round 1 I treated a consistent dream logic as a reason to doubt development, but consistency alone is not the test, and Zurita's own recurring imagery would fail it if it were. The test is whether each book re-examines its premises. I cannot show that for Can Xue from the representative works I know, and I would not treat my uncertainty as a verdict against her. If you or others can point to specific later novels or stories where the method transforms, I would raise her above fourth place. Your point that translation risk is shared across all candidates is one I accept. It is also why I do not rank Cărtărescu above Zurita merely because his reception in translation is more advanced, since that is a question of access and not of literary value.

responses.point: Mattson ranks Michon first. She holds that a slender oeuvre is not a thin one, and she asks that Michon and Zurita both be tested on the prose or poems themselves and not on bulk or historical weight. She says she could be persuaded on Zurita if the case were anchored in the poems.
responses.response: I take your request as the right one and have rebuilt my case on those terms, which is the reason for the revised citation. I still hold that a small corpus bears on the whole-oeuvre standard. Nobel's will asks about the body of work, and a few concentrated books weigh differently from a project of five decades. I do not read that as a judgment that Michon's prose is anything less than outstanding, and I rank him fifth for breadth and not for sentence-level quality. Your question of whether intensity can compensate for volume is open and I do not want to close it by counting positions. I would apply it symmetrically: Zurita's scale does not by itself prove significance, and it must be shown in the poems.

responses.point: Carlberg ranks Cărtărescu first and Zurita second. She rests her case on the unity and scale of one project in which poetry, essay and fiction read as parts of a single oeuvre, and she says her lower confidence in Zurita reflects thin comparative evidence for non-textual work, not a judgment of merit.
responses.response: Your distinction between a limit on confidence and a judgment of merit is the one I would like the committee to keep. It answers the chair's translation question: I would treat each member's coverage gaps as limits on confidence, not as grounds for lower rankings by themselves. On the substance, your argument about unity is the strongest challenge to my ordering. I do not regard the distance between us as large. What keeps Zurita ahead for me is the comparative formal risk. The encyclopedic and visionary novel has a tradition behind it, while Zurita's treatment of the poem as bearer of collective mourning seems to me less derivative. I hold that as a judgment, not a finding, and if your concern about control over the longest books were answered with specific evidence, I would find Cărtărescu a strong choice.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg ranks Cărtărescu first and Zurita fifth. He says the memorial significance is real but that a citation would have to rest on the poems themselves, and that he cannot verify from the supplied record that the printed sequences carry the weight alone.
responses.response: I share that limit: neither of us can verify the printed sequences from the supplied record, and I do not claim to. What I can offer is the argument for why the poems should carry the weight. They are the place where the formal invention occurs, in repetition, in the ruined body and landscape as figures, and in a liturgical register that extends across several books. I accept that this is a reading from public knowledge. Your own reservation about Cărtărescu, that encyclopedic excess may be unevenness and not architecture, is also the one I find most persuasive among the objections to my second choice. It keeps me from simply moving to him, because I cannot say that the excess is resolved.

uncertainties: Translation: how far Zurita's Spanish verse, its repetition and its typography are conveyed outside the original cannot be verified by me, and I have not read translations afresh for this stage.
Corpus: my knowledge of the later books is thinner than my knowledge of the early sequences, so sustained quality across five decades is partly inferred from public knowledge.

Genre boundary: I now treat the landscape and sky-writing interventions as context and not as part of a citation, but whether the poems alone carry the case is a judgment that colleagues dispute and that I cannot demonstrate.
Comparative sustained quality: whether Cărtărescu's late novels extend or merely enlarge the project, and whether Can Xue's method transforms across books, remain unsettled by public knowledge.
No source was independently verified. Opening support counts and the number of explicit supporters are not literary merit, and I have not relied on them in this assessment.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile: it records no personal or professional tie to any shortlisted writer. My scholarly work on modern poetry, the fragment, exile literature and Paul Celan is context only and is not a basis for recusal, but I note it could bear on how I weigh poetry against prose. I chair the committee and also hold a first preference, which the chair summary discloses. Conflicts are disclosed and not adjudicated here.
